newsitem.title: LATVIA: Baltic states cautiously welcome Russia-NATO pact.
newsitem.headline: Baltic states cautiously welcome Russia-NATO pact.

text.p: Officials in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania cautiously welcomed an agreement between Russia and NATO on Wednesday and reiterated that they were determined to join the western military alliance despite any objections from Moscow.
NATO and Russia reached an agreement in Moscow aimed at minimising Russia's security fears once NATO expands to include former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe.
"The very fact that NATO and Russia are cooperating is good...so long as they do not use Baltic membership (in NATO) as a bargaining chip," a senior Latvian diplomat told Reuters.
"But we are confident that no (such) deal has been struck," he said.
"We (the Baltic states) continue to aspire for an early invitation to join the alliance," he added.

The small Baltic countries believe that only NATO's protective embrace can shield them from a potentially hostile Russia, which has ruled them, often with an iron fist, for most of the last 200 years.
Suspicion of Moscow still runs deep in the Baltics, which were forcefully annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 after only decades of independence.

NATO is expected to name new candidates to join the 16-member alliance at a summit in Madrid in July. The likeliest countries are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, with Romania and Slovenia viewed as long-shots.
Diplomats and analysts have all but written the Baltics out of the first round of the organisation's enlargement on the grounds that such a move would be seen by Russia as a provocation.
Russia opposes NATO's plans to move east and is particularly sensitive about the Baltics, which formed its western flank during the Cold War and are still home to large Russian minorities.
"It is difficult to imagine that the agreement reached today does not touch on us (the Baltics)," Lithuanian indpendence hero and parliamentary chairman Vytautas Landsbergis told Reuters.
"As future NATO members, we would like to see the text of the agreement before it is signed in Paris on May 27," he said.
"The fact that Russia and NATO have made a step in developing their relations is positive," a spokesperson for Estonia's foreign ministry told Reuters.

But Estonian President Lennart Meri, on a visit to Hungary, invoked images from the Cold War, saying that Russia was still "an evil empire" and urging former Soviet republics and Warsaw Pact states to challenge it.
